analysis.one_liner: Restores full Social Security benefits to retirees who also earn government pensions.
analysis.headline: Despite 264 bipartisan cosponsors and majority support in the House, the bill never left committee and received no vote before Congress ended in January 2021.
analysis.plain_summary: Right now, people who worked jobs where Social Security taxes were withheld and then earned a pension from a government job where they were not — teachers, police officers, firefighters, some federal workers — can have their Social Security benefits cut by two rules called the windfall elimination provision and the government pension offset. This bill repeals both rules. About 3 million retirees and surviving spouses would get larger checks. It was introduced with near-majority support from both parties but was never given a vote.
analysis.who_benefits: Roughly 3 million retired and disabled public workers and their surviving spouses — mostly teachers, police officers, firefighters, and federal employees hired under pension systems that do not withhold Social Security taxes — who currently have their earned Social Security benefits reduced under the windfall elimination provision, or their spousal and survivor benefits reduced under the government pension offset.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Retired teachers, police, firefighters, federal workers

how_it_helps.text: The bill repeals the windfall elimination provision, which in some cases cuts the Social Security benefits of people who also receive a pension from an employer that did not withhold Social Security taxes.
It repeals the government pension offset, which in various cases reduces Social Security benefits for spouses, widows, and widowers who also receive government pensions of their own.
The repeal applies to benefits payable for months after December 2019, and directs the Social Security Commissioner to adjust benefit amounts accordingly.

analysis.who_pays: Social Security itself. Removing the offsets means the trust fund pays out more, which modestly speeds up its projected depletion date and slightly increases the pressure on future benefit or revenue decisions. Every dollar of offset that is repealed goes out as a benefit rather than staying in the system.

drawbacks.text: Repealing the offsets adds to Social Security's financing gap: the offsets exist in part because the affected workers did not pay Social Security taxes on their government pension earnings, so repeal raises benefits without a matching source of revenue, modestly hastening the day the trust fund can pay only a portion of promised benefits.

The windfall elimination provision attempts to keep Social Security's benefit formula from being more generous, proportionally, to someone whose non-covered pension years made their earnings look 'low' than it is to a lifelong low-wage worker who did pay in; repeal removes that adjustment entirely rather than replacing it with a fairer formula.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For the affected retirees, the benefit is concrete and large: they paid into Social Security during part of their careers and currently see those earned benefits sharply reduced, in some cases to near zero for survivor benefits. The cost is real but diffuse — a faster-drawing-down trust fund shared by everyone — and Congress chose to impose that cost on no one at all by doing nothing. A bill that replaced the offsets with a proportional formula (as later proposals have tried) would address critics' fairness concerns while still restoring benefits.

outcome.mechanism: The bill sat in the Ways and Means Committee and its Social Security subcommittee for two years and was never given a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote before Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rodney Davis introduced the bill on January 3, 2019, and it was referred to the House Committee on Ways and Means.
It gathered 264 cosponsors — 203 of 231 House Democrats and 61 of 197 House Republicans — which is more than a majority of the full House.
On January 31, 2019 it was referred to the Subcommittee on Social Security, and no further action was taken for the rest of the Congress.
The bill never received a committee vote or a floor vote and died when the 116th Congress ended on January 3, 2021.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The Social Security trust fund keeps the money the offsets currently withhold, and the committee leadership that never scheduled action avoids a vote on a payroll-funded benefit expansion. The roughly 3 million retirees and widows who would have gained are left with nothing.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Committee leadership and trust fund reserves

for.name: Rodney Davis
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on January 3, 2019, with 19 original cosponsors from both parties.

for.name: 203 of 231 House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, making up more than half of its 264 total cosponsors.

for.name: 61 of 197 House Republicans
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, adding bipartisan support beyond the Democratic majority.

against.name: Richard Neal
against.role: Chair, House Ways and Means Committee
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a committee markup or reported the bill, leaving it in the Social Security subcommittee for the full two years.

sides.party_line_note: Support was overwhelmingly bipartisan — 203 of 231 Democrats and 61 of 197 Republicans cosponsored — and no one voted against it; the bill died from inaction, not opposition.

industries.industry: Public-sector retirees and their labor unions
industries.note: Teachers, police, firefighters and the unions representing them have pushed for years to repeal the offsets; their members would have directly received the restored benefits. This is a group benefit, not a revenue stream, so their interest runs alongside the retirees it serves.

Repeal would have increased trust fund outlays for months after December 2019, modestly hastening projected depletion — a cost borne diffusely by future beneficiaries and taxpayers rather than by any industry.
